strengths: The paper presents a unified non-asymptotic regret analysis for online reinforcement learning in continuous state and action spaces, covering three distinct model classes: finite candidate models (achieving O(ln(N) + ln(m)) regret), infinite-dimensional normed function spaces via metric entropy/packing numbers, and compact parametric families (achieving O(sqrt(N p)) regret).

The paper rigorously addresses the critical issue of state boundedness and transient behavior in non-episodic continuous control with unbounded Gaussian noise, deriving explicit non-asymptotic bounds on the second moment of the state trajectory using a Lyapunov-based analysis.

The algorithmic formulation is conceptually elegant: it avoids optimistic upper-confidence-bound policy synthesis by decoupling estimation (via softmax/posterior sampling with decaying excitation) and certainty-equivalent control.
The manuscript is well-structured and clearly written, with comprehensive mathematical derivations provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation does not evaluate any nonlinear dynamical systems. While the central premise and theoretical framing of the paper focus on continuous nonlinear control, the numerical experiments in Section B are restricted to a linear time-invariant (LTI) system (decoupled leaky integrators) where discrete-time algebraic Riccati equations can be solved via standard linear quadratic regulator tools.

The assumptions required for the regret bounds are quite strong for general nonlinear systems: (i) Persistence of Excitation (Assumptions 3, 4, 6) is assumed to hold uniformly across all candidate feedback policies, which may fail if an incorrect policy drives the system into uninformative regions; (ii) The existence of a globally smooth cost-to-go function V with uniform quadratic growth (Assumptions 1, 2, 5, 7) is well-understood for linear-quadratic settings, but rarely satisfied globally for general nonlinear systems with unbounded noise.

The framework relies heavily on having pre-computed or easily accessible candidate policies mu^i / mu_theta for each candidate model. For general nonlinear dynamical systems, computing optimal or near-optimal infinite-horizon feedback policies offline is computationally prohibitive (curse of dimensionality in dynamic programming).

There are minor organizational and presentation issues in the appendix; for example, the heading of Section B.2 is labeled 'Setting S2' but actually discusses the setup and results for Setting S3 (parametric LTI matrices with p = 500 parameters).

strengths: Unifies multi-model adaptive control concepts with non-asymptotic online regret analysis for continuous state-action spaces.

Provides clean and rigorous Lyapunov-based regret analysis across three distinct model classes: finite model sets ($O(\ln N + \ln m)$ regret), non-parametric function classes via metric packing ($O(N\epsilon^2 + \ln(m(\epsilon))/\epsilon^2)$), and compact parametric families ($O(\sqrt{Np})$).

Explicitly addresses the crucial control-theoretic concern of state boundedness and stability by establishing uniform non-asymptotic bounds on the second moment of the state trajectories under stochastic disturbances.

The separation of model identification (via Bayesian/softmax posterior update) and certainty-equivalent control allows policy synthesis to be performed offline, avoiding expensive online re-optimization in settings where pre-computed policies are available.
weaknesses: The persistence of excitation condition (Assumption 3, and analogous Assumptions 4 and 6) is quite strong: it requires that every candidate model is distinguishable from the true model under *any* candidate policy $\mu^q$ in the set. In many nonlinear control problems, particular policies may keep the system confined to low-dimensional sub-manifolds where differences between dynamics remain unobservable without targeted active probing.

The algorithmic pipeline requires an exact or high-quality dynamic programming oracle to compute feedback policies $\mu^i$ for each candidate model. For general continuous nonlinear systems, solving the underlying infinite-horizon Bellman equation is computationally intractable (curse of dimensionality), limiting practical implementation to linear systems or low-dimensional approximations.

The empirical validation is conducted strictly on a linear time-invariant (LTI) system with discrete-time Riccati solvers (LQR). Despite the paper's primary focus on nonlinear dynamical systems, there are no experimental demonstrations on nonlinear benchmarks (e.g., inverted pendulum, Duffing oscillator, or robotic arms) to validate the transient behavior and excitation schedule in practice.

The noise excitation schedule $\sigma_{uk}^2$ relies on knowing problem-dependent constants such as the excitation parameter $c_e$ and Lipschitz constants, which are difficult to estimate or verify a priori for complex nonlinear systems.

strengths: Addresses an ambitious and fundamental problem in reinforcement learning: non-asymptotic policy regret bounds for continuous state-action spaces without episodic resets.

Bridges ideas from multi-model adaptive control (supervisory switching) and modern regret analysis, providing a unified viewpoint across finite model classes, non-parametric bounded function classes (via covering/packing), and parametric classes.
The theoretical framework provides explicit finite-time bounds and bounded second-moment state stability guarantees under the stated Lyapunov and excitation conditions.
The paper is mathematically rigorous and the appendix provides detailed proofs of the core propositions and lemmas.
weaknesses: Very strong persistence of excitation assumptions (Assumptions 3, 4, 6, and 8): The assumption that any applied candidate policy generates sufficient excitation to distinguish the true model from all other candidates is restrictive. In nonlinear systems, an incorrect or stabilizing candidate policy can easily drive the state to an attractor or equilibrium manifold where distinct models predict identical transitions, thereby stalling model identification.

Strict structural and global regularity requirements: The analysis relies on global Lipschitz continuity of the dynamics, smooth cost-to-go Lyapunov functions, and bounded growth under mismatched candidate controllers. In general nonlinear control, applying an incorrect policy can cause severe instability or finite-time escape, which are sidestepped here by strong global dissipation and Lipschitz bounds.

Mismatch between claims and empirical evaluation: While the paper repeatedly motivates the methodology with expressive function approximators such as neural networks and transformers, all numerical experiments are conducted exclusively on a simple linear time-invariant (LTI) system with algebraic Riccati solvers. There is no empirical validation on any truly nonlinear dynamical system.

High computational burden for general nonlinear classes: For non-linear parametric classes (Algorithm 3), the algorithm requires computing a certainty-equivalent optimal feedback policy for a newly sampled model at each epoch. In continuous-state nonlinear settings, computing such policies online or even offline is generally computationally intractable.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and challenging problem: online, non-episodic reinforcement learning over continuous state and action spaces with nonlinear dynamics and process noise, without requiring episodic resets.
Provides a unified, elegant algorithmic framework combining exponential weights (Hedge) / posterior sampling over models with certainty-equivalent control and injected excitation noise.

Derives rigorous, non-asymptotic frequentist policy-regret bounds across three key settings: finite model sets (logarithmic in horizon $N$ and model count $m$), infinite bounded function classes (via packing numbers), and parametric models ($O(\sqrt{d_u N p})$, matching known optimal LQR rates).

Explicitly establishes closed-loop stability and uniform second-moment bounds on state trajectories ($E[|x_k|^2] \le c_b$), which directly addresses the critical risk of instability and diverging transients during exploration in continuous dynamical systems.

The separation of model identification and certainty-equivalent control is modular and practical, enabling direct integration with established control tools such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) as demonstrated in the cart-pole swing-up simulation.
weaknesses: The persistence of excitation (PE) assumptions (Assumptions 3, 4, and 6) are central to establishing the fast $O(1/k^2)$ convergence of model selection. Although standard in classical system identification and adaptive control, establishing uniform PE a priori for general nonlinear systems can be difficult.

The Bellman-type dissipativity conditions (Assumptions 1, 5, and 7) require the existence of a smooth storage/value function $V$ satisfying specific dissipation bounds globally. While natural for LQR and dissipative systems, verifying these properties for complex general nonlinear systems is non-trivial.

Setting S2 (infinite cardinality) relies on online construction of an $\epsilon$-net and dynamic programming at each step, which is computationally intractable in practice. The authors acknowledge this as an information-theoretic sample complexity result, but the practical algorithmic scope remains centered on S1 and linear/Gaussian instances of S3.

The regret bound in Theorem 2.1 scales inversely with the model discrepancy $\Delta$ ($O(1/\Delta)$), meaning that if candidate models are closely clustered, the finite-model bound deteriorates (though mitigated by the $\epsilon$-discretization formulation in S2).

strengths: Addresses an important and notoriously difficult open problem: non-episodic, online reinforcement learning with continuous states and actions and nonlinear dynamics, establishing non-asymptotic frequentist policy-regret guarantees without state resets.

The proposed framework elegantly decouples model identification (via Hedge/posterior-sampling style updates on normalized prediction errors with injected exploration noise) from control synthesis (certainty equivalence / model predictive control), bypassing the computationally intractable confidence sets typically needed by optimism-based (OFU) approaches.

Provides sharp, near-optimal regret bounds across three distinct settings: $O(d_u(\ln N + \ln m)/\Delta)$ for finite model sets, packing-number based bounds for general normed spaces, and $O(\sqrt{d_u N p})$ for parametric model classes, gracefully recovering known minimax rates for linear-quadratic systems.

Rigorous treatment of closed-loop stability and boundedness of states: establishes finite second-moment bounds along closed-loop trajectories using dissipativity and Lyapunov analysis, addressing a crucial safety concern in continuous control.
Well-written manuscript with clear positioning relative to posterior sampling RL, multi-model adaptive control, online non-stochastic control, and the Decision-Estimation Coefficient (DEC) framework.
weaknesses: The persistence of excitation (PE) assumptions (Assumptions 3, 4, and 6) are quite strong in the nonlinear setting. They require that under *any* candidate policy $\mu^q$ perturbed by Gaussian excitation, every pair of distinct candidate models is separated in expected prediction error over $M$ steps. In nonlinear systems, an exploratory or stabilizing policy could steer the system into invariant manifolds or regions where dynamics are locally indistinguishable.

Computational tractability for general continuous/nonparametric model classes is limited: Setting S2 relies on an online greedy $\epsilon$-cover and dynamic programming at each update, which is computationally intractable in practice. For Setting S3 with nonlinear models (e.g., neural networks), sampling from $\exp(-\eta s_k(\theta))$ is generally non-log-concave and computationally challenging, and solving the corresponding nonlinear optimal control problem $\mu_\theta$ online is demanding.

Empirical evaluation is limited and illustrative: experiments are restricted to a stylized linear system and a simulated cart-pole swing-up with parametric mismatch (evaluating only Setting S1 with $m=500$). There are no empirical comparisons against relevant online control or reinforcement learning baselines.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and challenging open problem: nonasymptotic frequentist policy-regret guarantees for online, non-episodic reinforcement learning over continuous state-action spaces with nonlinear dynamics and no state resets.

Provides a clean and unified multi-model framework across three distinct regimes: a finite candidate model set (yielding logarithmic regret $O(\ln(N) + \ln(m))$), bounded nonparametric function classes characterized by packing numbers, and parametric families yielding $O(\sqrt{d_u N p})$ regret (recovering optimal bounds for LTI/LQR as a special case).

Technically rigorous bridge between online learning (Hedge/exponential weights with normalized loss functions) and control theory (dissipativity and Lyapunov stability analysis), decoupling system identification from certainty-equivalent control and avoiding intractable optimism-based confidence sets.
Explicitly guarantees closed-loop stability by establishing uniform nonasymptotic bounds on the second moment of state trajectories along the algorithm's execution.
Comprehensive mathematical proofs in the appendix and informative numerical simulations illustrating both linear systems and nonlinear cart-pole swing-up with non-realizable dynamics.
weaknesses: Relies on relatively strong structural and statistical assumptions, notably persistence of excitation (Assumptions 3, 4, and 6) and Bellman-type dissipation inequalities (Assumptions 1, 5, and 7); while standard or generic in linear control, these can be stringent and challenging to verify a priori for complex nonlinear systems.

Computational tractability is limited for some settings: Setting S2 requires constructing online $\epsilon$-packings and repeatedly solving dynamic programming problems over function spaces, and Setting S3 requires sampling from non-log-concave continuous posteriors when models are general nonlinear parametrizations.

The relaxation of the realizability assumption presented in Appendix G requires a candidate model to be uniformly closer to the true dynamics across the entire state-action space, which can be restrictive in misspecified model regimes.
